explanations.explanation: Whirlwinds, yes. The prophet says the invader comes "Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev, an invader comes from the desert, from a land of terror." (Isaiah 21:1) Picture a pan of cookies getting swept off the counter by one big spin. Nobody sees that coming, and that's the feeling.

Rivers are a fair guess, since rivers sweep things along too. But the text says "whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev." (Isaiah 21:1) The Negev is the dry south country, so a spinning wind fits better than water. A river in the desert would be the real surprise.

Flocks, like a bunch of sheep wandering in? Not this time, friend. The verse says the invader comes "Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev." (Isaiah 21:1) A flock moves along slow and fluffy, and a whirlwind moves FAST and nobody is fluffy.

That's it. The vision says, "Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media!" (Isaiah 21:2) Elam and Media are two nations, and they're the ones getting the orders here. A siege means surrounding a city and pressing in on it.

Going home would be a quiet ending, but that's not the order. The vision says, "Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media!" (Isaiah 21:2) These two are being sent forward, not sent back. Nobody in this vision is packing a suitcase.

Gifts and peace would be nice, like showing up with a box of cookies. But the vision doesn't go that way. It says, "Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media!" (Isaiah 21:2) A siege is the opposite of a gift basket.

Calm and relieved? Not even close, friend. The prophet says, "Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor." (Isaiah 21:3) He also says he's bewildered to hear and dismayed to see. This vision shook him, and he doesn't hide it.

Right, it's false. The prophet says, "Therefore my body is filled with anguish." (Isaiah 21:3) He's bewildered by what he hears and dismayed by what he sees. Nobody's kicking back with a cold drink after a vision like that.

Horror is right. The prophet says, "The twilight I desired has turned to horror." (Isaiah 21:4) Twilight is the soft end of the day, the part you'd want to enjoy. His went the other way, and I'd say that's a hard turn.

Rest would be lovely. Twilight sounds like rest, doesn't it? But the prophet says, "The twilight I desired has turned to horror." (Isaiah 21:4) His heart falters and fear makes him tremble, so there's no resting happening.

Glory sounds big and shiny, but that's not the word here. The prophet says, "The twilight I desired has turned to horror." (Isaiah 21:4) Right before it, he says his heart falters and fear makes him tremble. Trembling doesn't go with glory.

Yes, oil the shields. The call says, "Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!" (Isaiah 21:5) It comes right in the middle of the table, the carpet, the eating and the drinking. I think that's a loud way to say the party is about to get interrupted.
Laying down swords is the wrong direction. The call says, "Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!" (Isaiah 21:5) The princes are told to get up and get ready. Nobody here is being told to relax.

Opening the gates sounds like a welcome party, and the table is already set for one. But the call to the princes is, "Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!" (Isaiah 21:5) Shields are for getting ready, not for letting anybody stroll in.

That's the list. The Lord says the lookout will see "chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels." (Isaiah 21:7) That's a lot of traffic coming down one road. The lookout has plenty to keep his eyes on.

Ships would be a fine thing to watch for if this were a harbor. But the Lord's list is "chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels." (Isaiah 21:7) Everything on that list rolls or rides on dry land. Not a sail in sight.

Smoke on the hills is a good guess, but it's not on the list. The Lord says the lookout will see "chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels." (Isaiah 21:7) He's watching for travelers on the road. Smoke would be a whole other kind of news.
True. The Lord says, "he must be alert, fully alert." (Isaiah 21:7) That's the whole job. Half alert won't do it, friend, and neither will a nap.
It's actually true. The Lord tells the prophet the lookout "must be alert, fully alert." (Isaiah 21:7) No dozing and no looking at his phone. That man is fully on the job.

Fallen, and he says it twice. "Fallen, fallen is Babylon!" (Isaiah 21:9) Saying it twice makes it ring like a bell. The lookout watched day after day and night after night, and this was the news that came.
Won? Babylon is the one in trouble here. The answer to the lookout is, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon!" (Isaiah 21:9) The riders come in pairs, and the news they bring is a fall, not a victory.
Grown would be good news for Babylon, but that's not what the lookout hears. The answer is, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon!" (Isaiah 21:9) It's said twice, so it's hard to miss. Nobody here is growing.
True. The voice says, "All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!" (Isaiah 21:9) Those images couldn't even stay in one piece. That's a rough day for anyone who trusted them.
It's actually true. The verse says, "All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!" (Isaiah 21:9) They're not standing on a shelf or sitting in a temple. They're broken on the ground.

That's who he names. The prophet says, "I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel." (Isaiah 21:10) He's passing on what he heard, and he says where it came from. That's how a good messenger works.

Sargon, king of Assyria, is a big name, but he isn't the one the prophet names. The prophet says, "I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel." (Isaiah 21:10) The message comes from the LORD, not from any king.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is a fun pick, but this passage never names him. The prophet says, "I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel." (Isaiah 21:10) Babylon is the one falling in this passage, so its king wouldn't be the one handing out news.
